nameStory: The word 'horse' comes from the Old English 'hors,' which traces back thousands of years to ancient languages describing this magnificent animal. Humans have been so closely connected to horses for over 6,000 years that the name has remained remarkably unchanged across cultures and continents.
description: The domestic horse is a large, powerful mammal with a muscular body, long legs built for running, and a distinctive flowing mane and tail. These impressive animals typically stand 4-6 feet tall at the shoulder and can weigh anywhere from 800 to 2,000 pounds depending on the breed. Horses have a single hoof on each foot, large expressive eyes positioned on the sides of their head, and pointed, mobile ears that can swivel to catch sounds from all directions. Their coat comes in many colors including bay, chestnut, black, gray, and various spotted patterns.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Unmistakably large with a rectangular body profile, long muscular neck, and legs that seem impossibly thin for supporting such a massive frame. The head is elongated with a distinctive dished or straight facial profile.

idTips.label: Hooves
idTips.description: Single, large rounded hoof on each foot that makes a distinctive clip-clop sound on hard surfaces. Fresh hoofprints are circular to oval, about 4-6 inches across, and much larger than any wild animal tracks in New England.

idTips.label: Mane & Tail
idTips.description: Long, flowing hair cascades down the neck (mane) and forms a full tail that reaches nearly to the ground. The hair feels coarse and thick between your fingers, quite different from the shorter body coat.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen grazing with head down, but will quickly lift their head and prick their ears forward when alert. May run in powerful, rhythmic gaits and can sleep standing up, often resting one hind leg.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in fenced pastures, paddocks, or barns on farms and rural properties. Always associated with human habitation and agricultural areas, never truly wild in New England.

habitat: Domestic horses in New England are found on farms, horse properties, and riding facilities throughout rural and suburban areas. They live in fenced pastures with grass for grazing, often with access to barns or run-in sheds for shelter. You'll typically see them in rolling farmland, converted agricultural areas, and along rural roads where equestrian properties are common.

seasonality.spring: Horses shed their thick winter coats, leaving tufts of hair on fence posts and in pastures. Many mares give birth to foals during this season, so you might spot awkward-legged babies staying close to their mothers.
seasonality.summer: Horses have sleek, short coats and spend more time in shade during hot days. You'll often see them standing head-to-tail, using their tails to swish flies off each other's faces.
seasonality.fall: Coats begin thickening for winter, becoming fluffier and sometimes changing color slightly. Horses may be more active in the cooler weather after a sluggish summer.
seasonality.winter: Heavy, fuzzy winter coats make horses look much rounder and shaggier. Many wear waterproof blankets, and you'll see their warm breath creating steam clouds in cold air.

funFact: Horses can sleep standing up by locking their leg joints in place, but they actually need to lie down to achieve deep REM sleep - and they only need about 2-3 hours of this deep sleep per day, far less than humans!
confusionNotes: In New England, horses are sometimes confused with large ponies or draft animals like oxen from a distance. Remember that horses have single hooves (not split like cattle), flowing manes and tails, and a much more refined head shape than bovines.
contextualKnowledge: While horses evolved in North America millions of years ago, they went extinct here and were reintroduced by European settlers in the 1600s. All horses you see today are domestic animals - there are no truly wild horses in New England, though some feral populations exist in western states.
compareHints: Horses are the only members of the equine family commonly found in New England. They're much larger than their wild relatives like zebras and significantly bigger than donkeys or mules, with proportionally longer legs, more refined heads, and fuller manes and tails that flow freely rather than standing upright.
